column6: The shrine at Pian d’Civita is among the earliest evidence of Etruscan religious practice, in the Villanovan period.
The sanctuary at the Piazza d’Armi grew into a fully developed sanctuary.
A bronze statue base of 525–500 BCE at Campo della Fiera records a freedwoman’s dedication to a deity.

column3: Etruscan religious practice appears in the Villanovan period, with shrines at Tarquinia and Veii and cremation burial in urns with grave goods.
Greek gods and heroes such as Aritimi, Hercle and Pacha join the Etruscan pantheon in the Orientalizing Period.
Etruscan sanctuaries become increasingly monumental, with major temples, expensive offerings and animal sacrifice.
After the defeat in the Roman–Etruscan Wars (264 BCE), the Roman Senate adopts key elements of Etruscan religion, kept by haruspices and noble families of Etruscan descent.
In the last years of the Roman Republic the religion falls out of favour and is satirized by Cicero.
The Julio-Claudians keep some knowledge of the language and religion for a short time, then the practice ceases.
